newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Clinton used quiet diplomacy to score APEC points.
newsitem.headline: Clinton used quiet diplomacy to score APEC points.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton used a relatively new weapon in his diplomatic arsenal -- friendship -- to turn a potentially embarrassing setback into a triumph at the Asia-Pacific summit.
Clinton, who came to the White House four years ago with virtually no foreign policy experience, succeeded because he used quiet diplomacy based on his relationship with other leaders.
The man who once scoffed at the importance of former president George Bush's honed skills in foreign affairs now values them himself.

Before leaving Washington, senior officials made it clear they wanted the 18 members of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum, whose leaders held a one-day summit on Monday in Subic Bay, to endorse a call for doing away with tariffs on information technology.

In preliminary work at the APEC ministerial level, it was clear Clinton's mission had failed before it began. The ministers balked at using firm language that would have committed their governments to set the year 2000 as a target date.

With members of the U.S. delegation privately starting to search for ways to explain away the failure of the proposal, Clinton spent much of Sunday trying to enlist -- successfully, it turned out -- the help of fellow leaders.
One senior U.S. official, reviewing how the summit wound up formally endorsing Clinton's plan, credited the reversal to "the use of the relationships that he (Clinton) has developed".
Several officials pointed to the private talks Clinton held on Sunday with Philippine President Fidel Ramos and Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto.

The three leaders each worked on building a consensus, with Clinton stressing the benefits of doing away with tariffs for each of the countries in the region -- not just the largest producer, the United States.

"There were a lot of leaders that were happy to move forward with him and to come out with a very strong statement on this issue," said one obviously relieved high-ranking American official involved in many of the talks.
Before he left for Thailand, final stop on a 12-day trek through Hawaii, Australia and Asia, Clinton sounded euphoric with the final APEC declaration.
"This... agreement is a big deal and it is a product of determined, consistent diplomacy," he told workers at the U.S. embassy.
The trip to the Philippines also brought an agreement with Chinese President Jiang Zemin that offered a breakthrough in the effort to defuse still lingering Washington-Beijing tensions.
The two men agreed to begin an exchange of high-level visits leading to a Sino-U.S. summit in Washington in 1997 and one in Beijing the following year.

The Chinese have long pressed behind the scenes for a summit in Washington, something Clinton has declined to do until he felt there was headway -- or at least the potential for headway -- in trade disputes between the two countries.
He also has been pressing for an end to human rights abuses by Beijing, but has dropped his initial policy of linking other negotiations to civil liberties improvements.

The summit-exchange announcement sent a strong signal throughout the Pacific Rim that Clinton intends to be heavily engaged in the region and wants to end long-simmering tensions following his re-election on November 5 for a second term.
